The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them.

Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term.

The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.

He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.

During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.

If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.

As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".

"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.

She also said Law's motives were financial.

"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.

Electric minivans could be the ultimate in utility, with room for passengers, gear, and huge batteries. While VW's ID Buzz only gave us 200 miles of real-world driving on a charge in 2023, China's BYD has just announced a flagship purple peoplemover that can go an estimated 559 miles (900 km) on electricity.

Instead of purely looking forward with its headphone designs, Sony went back to its popular WH-1000XM4 design and made some improvements to make it even better. The 2026 version, called the WH-1000XM4C, sounds nearly as good as the pricier XM6 model (currently $348), but is down to $198 during Black Friday at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart. That’s $100 off their October launch price.

$299.99 $199.99 at Best Buy

There’s a reason why Sony went back to refine the XM4. Our former reviewer Chris Welch praised them for being super comfortable and for having close to perfect features for the price, especially compared to its successor, the XM3 (still my daily driver, for what it’s worth). The XM4s had better sound quality and noise cancellation, plus improved mics, multipoint connectivity, and a sensor that can detect when you remove them to automatically pause audio. Now, with the XM4C, there are further improvements, most notably a 10-band equalizer in the app (compared to the original XM4’s five-band) that my colleague John Higgins says really helped the headphones’ midrange frequencies open up.

These are a great buy, but they aren’t your only Sony headphones deal to consider right now. Sony’s WH-1000XM5 are available during Black Friday at Best Buy for $169, their lowest price yet from a major retailer. There are upsides and downsides to this model: They feature improved noise cancellation thanks to more mics, despite using the same ANC chip as the XM4C, but they can’t fold up as compactly, making them a little bigger to pack in your bag. Either one you choose, you’ll have some great headphones to listen to going into 2027.

items.summary: Kyriakos Axiotis，资深研究科学家，Thomas Fu，谷歌研究院首席工程师（来源：Hacker News·硅谷热榜）
items.content:
Kyriakos Axiotis，资深研究科学家，Thomas Fu，谷歌研究院首席工程师

我们提出了 DeepCrossAttention (DCA)，这是一种通过使用可学习权重和深度交叉注意力来动态组合前一层的输出来增强变压器网络的架构，从而防止传统残差连接中出现的信息稀释。我们在 ICML 2025 论文中提出，这种架构改进使模型能够以可忽略的参数增加达到相同质量，速度提高三倍。

将传统的深度学习模型想象成一场巨大的“电话”游戏：数据一层又一层地传递，每一层都会稍微改变信息。如果网络有数十或数百层，则原始学习信号在到达所有层时可能会严重退化或丢失，这在人工智能中被称为梯度消失问题。

为了克服这一挑战并实现数十或数百层网络的训练，变压器严重依赖剩余连接，也称为“跳过”连接，其作用就像信息高速公路或捷径。原始输入的副本不会强制数据专门通过复杂的层，而是直接跳过该层并直接添加到其输出中。这确保了模型始终

Kyriakos Axiotis, Staff Research Scientist, and Thomas Fu, Principal Engineer, Google Research

We present DeepCrossAttention (DCA), an architecture that enhances transformer networks by using learnable weights and depth-wise cross-attention to dynamically combine outputs from previous layers, preventing the information dilution seen in traditional residual connections. Presented in our ICML 2025 paper, this architectural improvement allows models to achieve the same quality up to three times faster with a negligible increase in parameters.

Think of a traditional deep learning model like a giant game of "Telephone": data passes through layer after layer, with each layer changing the information slightly. If a network has dozens or hundreds of layers, the original learning signal can become severely degraded or lost by the time it reaches all layers, which is known as the vanishing gradient problem in AI.

To overcome this challenge and enable the training of networks with dozens or hundreds of layers, transformers rely heavily on residual connections, also known as “skip” connections, which act like an information highway or a shortcut. Instead of forcing the data to pass exclusively through the complicated layer, a duplicate copy of the original input skips right past this layer and is added directly to its output. This ensures that the model always has the original raw data to refer back to.

The standard residual connection implements a simple operation: point-wise summation of a layer's output with its input. While computationally efficient, this simple process has a key limitation: it treats all prior representations with equal weight, leading to information dilution in deep networks. As features propagate through many layers, specific, high-resolution details from earlier layers can be averaged out or distorted, making it difficult for the network to selectively retrieve them. This forces the network to recompute them, reducing learning efficiency.

In our ICML 2025 paper, "DeepCrossAttention: Supercharging Transformer Residual Connections," we studied the shortcomings of the traditional residual architecture and introduced DeepCrossAttention (DCA), which generalizes residual connections by allowing each layer to dynamically select and route features from the history of preceding layers. By allowing the model to dynamically choose which previous layers are most important at any given moment, DCA achieves comparable or improved learning, while reducing the number of parameters needed by up to 30-40%.

Instead of treating skip connections as a rigid, additive pipeline, DCA reframes residual learning as a dynamic routing problem. Rather than passing all prior layers forward with equal weight, DCA introduces a lightweight, layer-wise module that decides how to best combine previous embeddings on a per-token basis.

An official inspects the partially submerged tanker - the rescue operation is expected to be challenging

A tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel which capsized off the holiday island of Ibiza on Thursday will be towed to the port of Cartagena, officials in Spain say.

All 17 of the Malta-registered Med Emre's crew members were rescued but the chief engineer later died in hospital. Six people were treated for minor injuries.

There had been concerns of a major oil spillage in the western Mediterranean but an inspection showed that the ship's fuel tanks are intact. An investigation is under way into what happened.

The vessel had been travelling from Algeciras near Gibraltar to Barcelona and is expected to arrive in Cartagena on Monday in what is being seen as a challenging rescue operation.

In a statement on Friday, the Spanish transport ministry said the tanker would be towed to Cartagena "as it is the only one [port] that meets the technical requirements to carry out cargo extraction and repair work".

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told Cadena SER radio network he hoped the tanker could be taken to port "in the coming hours, in the coming days".

"The information suggests that, indeed... this leak is not happening", he added.

The Spanish authorities provided no details about how the diesel would be extracted.

Meanwhile, pictures have emerged showing emergency workers inspecting the tanker's hull.

RICHMOND, Va. – Today, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones took a significant step in holding operators of X and its AI tool, Grok, accountable for knowingly failing to protect Virginians, while falsely promoting the safety of its platform and AI tool.

In the lawsuit, the Commonwealth of Virginia alleges that SpaceX, the telecommunications and space transportation conglomerate that operates the social network X and its artificial intelligence company, xAI (now called “SpaceX Super Intelligence”), and developed the Grok family of large language models, failed to prevent Grok from generating sexualized images of people, including children, without their knowledge or consent—while simultaneously promoting the safety of the social media platform and AI tool. The Grok-generated content includes non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII), other non-consensual sexualized images, and Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM). Today’s suit was filed in collaboration with Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, who filed a separate but similar action.

“This lawsuit is about seeking justice for the millions of Virginians who maintain accounts on X and were misled by the company’s false reassurances that their data and images would be safe on the platform,” said Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones. “When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it. Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.”

With a single existing photograph, Grok could, and did, fabricate a realistic image or video of a person nude, or partially nude, or engaged in sexual activity, all without the individual’s knowledge or consent. This violation is not acceptable.

I wrote this book between 2011 and 2015. At the time, I expected AGI systems based on neural networks to be many decades away, but to bring remarkable benefits for humanity. I also expected significant challenges, but believed it likely that, as with other technologies, those challenges would be addressed as the capabilities were developed.

My views have changed. With the extraordinarily reckless behaviour of the frontier labs, the systems have raced ahead much faster than I expected1, giving humanity far too little time to meet the challenges. Although the systems genuinely will bring — indeed, already are bringing — many wonders, they also pose a significant risk of catastrophe. The frontier labs are knowingly endangering all of humanity. I've written about why I believe this at length, most recently in “Which Future?”. Two brief thoughts are below.

I don't wish to help (even in a very small way) train people to contribute to this work, and so I've taken the book down.

What follows are two brief remarks: one on the nature of the threat posed by ASI, and another on the ethical justification for working on frontier AI.

The most common argument for AI existential risk, developed by Nick Bostrom and Eliezer Yudkowsky, is loss of control of the future to advanced AI systems2. I believe this concern should be understood as one instance of a more fundamental issue. That issue is whether we will discover technologies latent in nature which are easy and inexpensive to develop, catastrophic in outcome, and beyond our capacity to defend against. If such “progress” in technology were happening slowly, our social institutions might successfully develop defences. But it seems likely that ASI will cause a sudden explosion of such destructive technologies, with insufficient time to adapt.

A historical example to help prime intuition is fire. It is easy to make and extremely difficult to defend against. We have a one-cent technology, the matchstick, which requires hundreds of billions of dollars each year to defend against, as well as a whole apparatus of social institutions, technology, infrastructure and law3. AI systems will enable technologies which are far more destructive than matches. Understandably, people skeptical of catastrophic risks want these supposed threats spelled out in detail. This is intrinsically difficult, because we can't reliably anticipate future science and technology. While it is common to speculate about biothreats, I expect the worst threats will be technologies we haven't yet imagined. Nature is, after all, more imaginative than we.

Now suppose that ASI enables a 100-times speed-up in technological progress, without a matching change in the rate of social progress or social defenses. To get a sense of what the impact of such a speed-up would be, imagine that all the technological problems that occurred in the 20th century had occurred in the year 1901: the atomic bomb, the hydrogen bomb, the ICBM, chemical weapons, biological weapons, the CFC-caused ozone hole, sulfuric acid rain, climate change, and many more. While we've dealt well with some of these problems, it required decades of concerted work to develop the social institutions and agreements needed for an effective response. Again, defence is often much harder than offence, and relies on different systems. Of course, such a speed-up would also have brought the century's wonders all at once. But imagine another such set of equally difficult problems arising in 1902, and then 1903, and then 1904, and so on. I believe it would have made the world extraordinarily unstable and eventually liable to collapse.

The issue with ASI, then, is the destructive power latent in nature. It doesn't matter whether that power is wielded by humans or by out-of-control machines4. I make this point because many people mistakenly believe that loss of control to such rogue machines is the fundamental issue. This leads them to treat AI safety as principally a technical problem, which can be addressed by “aligning” individual systems. Unfortunately, it cannot. Furthermore, such a view makes it seem as though the labs are the primary places where safety can be addressed. But such technical alignment is mostly market-supplied safety, which makes the systems more palatable to consumers and governments. It speeds development, and thus makes the fundamental underlying problem worse, while only addressing an (important) subsidiary problem.

My view isn't popular, in part because it makes the problem of technology about making the entire world safe, not only about aligning particular AI systems. Indeed, even in a future where humanity no longer existed, the same problem would afflict any successor AI civilization: it would have to defend itself against these destructive capacities. Similarly, it afflicts any model of the future based on human uplift, through brain-computer interfaces and similar augmentation: the issue isn't which substrate intelligence runs on, but the dual-use nature of deep understanding of reality5. In some sense, it's a question of whether sentience in the cosmos is compatible with advanced understanding of nature. Of course, I hope it is compatible. But rushing the technology while the broader social response lags seems likely to result in failure on our particular planet.

Many people inside the frontier AI labs genuinely believe AI systems may pose a catastrophic threat. Why then do they help build such systems? They often justify their participation by arguing that it's better they do it than someone else does. Dario Amodei, for example, has made versions of this argument often: “If one company does not build it, others will do so nearly as fast”6; “Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers”7; and Anthropic itself gives, as its founding rationale, “if powerful AI is coming regardless, Anthropic believes it's better to have safety-focused labs at the frontier than to cede that ground to developers less focused on safety”8.

How New York reacted to postponement of Macy's parade

Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.

"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.

Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (£267,000) in just a few hours.

Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.

On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.

The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.

The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.

Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.

当您从波兰边境驱车八小时到达基辅时，奇怪的事情发生了：您手机上的时钟变成了午夜。这并不是真正针对手机的——它似乎是一个更广泛战略的一部分，目的是迷惑俄罗斯发射的导弹和无人机。

不过，除了这样的小事之外，基辅乍一看似乎相当正常。当警报器开始鸣响，人们检查手机上的通知时，你就会清楚地意识到战争正在打响，这些通知告诉他们有红色警报，导弹正在袭来。您甚至可以购买一些小工具来显示无人机来自哪个方向以及它们的类型。

Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

Kyiv is entering its fourth winter following Russia's full-scale invasion

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.

Budget carrier Norse Atlantic filed for bankruptcy Friday, saying it failed to secure funding after soaring fuel costs strained the company's operations throughout the year.

Its parent company, Norse Atlantic ASA, concluded that the Norwegian carrier no longer has a basis to continue operations.

"Despite extensive efforts, the Company has so far not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs," the firm said in a statement Friday.

It comes days after Norse said it's facing a "critical financial situation" and was considering its options from a strategic takeover to ACMI contracts, which refer to short-term capacity leasing. The company's shares closed 85% lower on Wednesday.

The board has now filed a bankruptcy petition with the Agder District Court, where a trustee will be appointed to manage the process further.

"The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the Company and the Group to find a solution," Norse Atlantic CEO Eivind Roald said.

"We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners. The Board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations," Roald added.

The company has canceled all flights, and ticket sales have been discontinued.

Norse was founded in March 2021 and offered cheap flights between Europe, North America, Africa and Asia.

The Iran war began on Feb. 28 and caused jet fuel prices to skyrocket, forcing airlines around the world to grapple with higher costs. Prices are now up nearly 72% to $155 per barrel year-on-year as of the week ending Nov. 20, according to the International Air Transport Association's Jet Fuel Price Monitor.

U.S. equities rose on Friday as investors wrapped up a turbulent, holiday-shortened trading week.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average was higher by 591.99 points, or 1.18%, to close at 50,774.94. The S&P 500 added 1.6% to end the day at 7,297.49, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced 2.31% to 24,129.50. The moves come amid a volatile week during an even more volatile month.

Technology stocks supported Friday's bounce. "Magnificent Seven" members Meta Platforms and Amazon popped more than 3% and about 4%, respectively, while chipmaker Broadcom increased almost 4%. Shares of artificial intelligence lab Anthropic added nearly 11%.

The major U.S. stock benchmarks posted strong weekly gains. The Dow and S&P 500 were both up more than 5%. The former notched its biggest weekly advance since October 2022, while the latter posted its best week since April 2025. The Nasdaq has surged more than 6%, scoring its largest weekly gain since April.

The week kicked off with Jensen Huang getting reinstated as CEO at Nvidia, a move that sent the stock up 31% during Monday's session and drove the S&P 500 and Nasdaq to post their best days since April 2025. The Dow advanced more than 1,400 points, or roughly 3%.

Since then, however, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq have come under pressure as Nvidia and other AI-related stocks have given back some of Monday's gains.

Prior to Huang's departure earlier this month, sentiment toward the AI trade was already downbeat, with investors growing concerned about debt financing, signs of moderation in capital expenditures and Democratic wins in the midterm elections resulting in a slowdown in data center development.

But Ben Fulton of WEBs Investments believes the fears surrounding AI, except for those regarding debt financing, are "a bit overblown," noting that the "biggest risk" is whether AI companies can "keep funding the growth they need." At the same time, he doesn't think investors can "afford to be out of the AI story."

"The risk seems to be on the upside right now," the CEO said. "You don't want to be short this market, at least the AI names."

To be sure, others believe that while there are long-term anxieties with the AI trade, the recent weakness in the market has had more to do with the prospect of the Federal Reserve raising interest rates. The latest personal consumption expenditures price index reading this week reinforced traders' expectations for multiple hikes over the coming months.

Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".

The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

I am a professional physicist and I shuffle symbols in equations and mathematical expressions all day long. During my PhD (almost 20 years ago) I noticed that it is as if the symbols have their own 'physics', which makes the wrong moves impossible and the right ones obvious.

So I created DragDropMath, where you can learn how to simplify mathematical expressions and how to solve equations by dragging symbols around, and only correct moves are allowed, so you get to feel what's right without experiencing (and so learning) wrong moves.

I always wanted to make this, but life got in the way. Then a few weeks ago I saw declarative dragging (https://declarative-dragging.github.io/) on the front page of HN and the spark came back!

It took quite a few rounds to get the feel right, but I think it's close to what happens in my mind when I mentally manipulate these expressions.

A few more points: - There are no ads, no trackers, no accounts (it's a static website and progress is saved in the browser cache). - Teachers can create their own problem sets, encoded in the link. - I plan to add more chapters (trigonometry, complex numbers, some calculus) but I first need to figure out the 'right' mode of interaction. - I just started working on the experience from mobile, so there may still be some rough edges there

I'm curious to know what you think, if you have suggestions for content, if you spot anything that I should fix, if you have feature requests! Thank you in advance

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves

A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.

Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.

Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.

Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.

Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.

The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.

Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.

The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the cases against him.

Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.

The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.

Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.

The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.

Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority."

The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.

On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.

The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.

While the majority of the seven justices found that Quebec's law is largely valid, some dissented to parts of the decision.

Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Nicholas Kasirer wrote that the notwithstanding clause "cannot be used to authorize laws that are incompatible with the fundamental character of Canada as a free and democratic country".
